questions.q: You have edited a file but have not run git add. Where does that change live?

a.why: Your ordinary files. Git can see the change but has recorded nothing, which is why this is the one state Git cannot get back for you.
Not yet. Nothing reaches the staging area until you add it.
No. The repository only holds what you have committed.
No. Nothing leaves your machine until you push, and nothing is even committed yet.

questions.q: Which command moves what you have staged into your history?

a.why: add moves changes into the staging area, one step earlier.
commit turns the staged snapshot into a permanent one and moves your branch label onto it.
push copies commits you have already made to a remote.
stash puts changes on a shelf instead of recording them.

questions.q: A branch, in Git, is best described as:

a.why: Nothing is copied. That is why branching is instant even on a huge repository.

a.t: A movable label pointing at one commit
a.why: That is the whole secret. Committing moves the label forward; creating a branch just adds another label.
There is a file recording where it points, but the branch itself is only that pointer.
A branch protects nothing on its own; it is a pointer, not a copy.

questions.q: You run git fetch. What just changed?

a.why: No. That is the point of fetch: your working tree is untouched.
No. Your own branch never moves on a fetch.
Fetch updates your origin/* labels and nothing else. Pull is fetch plus a merge, which is the part that can surprise you.
Something did change: your origin/* labels now show where the remote actually is.

questions.q: You ran git reset --hard and lost a commit you wanted. It is:

a.why: Almost never true, and believing it causes a lot of unnecessary panic.

a.t: Still there, and the reflog can find it
a.why: Reset moves a label; it does not delete commits. git reflog lists where HEAD has been, and resetting back to that hash brings the work home.
It may not have been pushed at all, and you still would not have lost it.
Git keeps its own safety net. The reflog is that net.

questions.q: What does a pull request actually contain?

a.t: A copy of your changed files
a.why: No copying happens. The commits are already on GitHub before the pull request exists.

a.t: A request to merge a branch that is already pushed
a.why: That is all it is: your branch, proposed into another, with somewhere for people to talk about it.

a.t: A patch file emailed to the maintainer
a.why: That is the older mailing-list workflow. Git supports it, but it is not what a pull request is.
A pull request protects nothing. Your branch is safe because you pushed it, not because you proposed it.

questions.q: Your pull request was merged on GitHub. Your local main now:

a.why: It does not. Nothing reaches your machine on its own.

a.t: Does not have it until you pull
a.why: Two different places moved: GitHub's main, and later yours. This is the step people forget, and then wonder why their main looks stale.

a.t: Is broken and needs a fresh clone
a.why: Nothing is broken. It is simply behind.

a.t: Updates the next time you commit
a.why: Committing adds to your history; it never brings anything down from GitHub.

questions.q: Your push is rejected as non-fast-forward. The right first move is:

a.why: This is the answer that loses somebody's work. Force overwrites the commits you have not seen.
The rejection means origin has work you do not. Bring it in, resolve anything that conflicts, then push.

a.t: Delete the branch and start over
a.why: Nothing is wrong with your branch; it is just missing a commit from someone else.
A fresh clone throws away your work to avoid a one-command fix.

a.t: A branch with a different name
a.why: A branch lives in one repository. A fork is a separate repository.

a.t: Your own copy of someone else's repository, on GitHub
a.why: It is a server-side copy under your account, which is how you contribute somewhere you cannot push to directly.
That is a clone. A fork exists on GitHub, and you usually clone your fork afterwards.

a.t: A permanent split from the original
a.why: It can be, but usually a fork stays connected: you sync from upstream and send pull requests back.
